content: An infant of a diabetic mother (IDM) refers to a baby born to a mother who had consistently high blood sugar (glucose) levels during pregnancy. Symptoms of an Infant of a Diabetic Mother: These infants are often larger than expected for their gestational age. Additional symptoms may include: Bluish or mottled skin coloration, rapid heart rate, and rapid breathing, which may indicate immature lungs or heart failure. Newborn jaundice, characterized by yellowing of the skin. Poor feeding, lethargy, and a weak cry, which are signs of severe low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). A puffy face. A reddish appearance of the skin. Tremors or shaking shortly after birth. Causes of Infant of a Diabetic Mother: High blood sugar levels in pregnant women can have specific effects on their infants. These babies are generally larger than average and may have enlarged organs, particularly the liver, adrenal glands, and heart. These infants may experience episodes of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) shortly after birth due to increased insulin production. Insulin is a hormone that moves glucose from the blood into body tissues. Close monitoring of the infant's blood sugar levels is necessary. Poorly controlled diabetes in the mother increases the risk of miscarriage or stillbirth. If the mother had diabetes before pregnancy and it was not well-controlled, the infant has a higher risk of birth defects. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If you are pregnant and receiving regular prenatal care, routine testing will detect gestational diabetes. If you are pregnant and have diabetes that is difficult to control, contact your doctor immediately. If you are pregnant and not receiving prenatal care, schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider or contact the State Board of Health for assistance in obtaining prenatal care. Diagnosis: An ultrasound performed in the later months of pregnancy may reveal that the baby is larger than expected for its gestational age. Lung maturity testing may be conducted on the amniotic fluid if delivery is being considered more than a week before the due date. After birth, tests may show that the infant has low blood sugar and low blood calcium levels. An echocardiogram may reveal an abnormally large heart, which can lead to heart failure. Treatment Options: All infants born to mothers with diabetes should be tested for low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), even if they show no symptoms. If an infant experiences an episode of low blood sugar, blood sugar levels will be monitored over several days until they stabilize with normal feedings. Early feedings may prevent low blood sugar in mild cases. Persistent low blood sugar is treated with glucose administered intravenously. In rare cases, the infant may require breathing support or medications to address other effects of diabetes. High bilirubin levels are treated with phototherapy (light therapy) or, in rare cases, an exchange transfusion, where the baby's blood is replaced with donor blood. Prognosis: Improved diabetes management and early recognition of gestational diabetes have reduced the number and severity of complications in infants born to diabetic mothers. Most symptoms in the infant resolve within a few weeks. However, an enlarged heart may take several months to improve. Possible Complications: Congenital heart defects. Heart failure. High bilirubin levels (hyperbilirubinemia), which can cause permanent brain damage. Immature lungs. Neonatal polycythemia (an excess of red blood cells), which can lead to blood vessel blockages or hyperbilirubinemia. Severe low blood sugar, which may result in permanent brain damage. Small left colon syndrome, which causes symptoms of intestinal blockage. Stillbirth. Prevention: To prevent complications, the mother requires supportive care throughout pregnancy. Good blood sugar control and early diagnosis of gestational diabetes can prevent many problems associated with this condition. Lung maturity testing may help prevent breathing complications if delivery is planned more than a week before the due date. Careful monitoring of the infant during the first 24 hours after birth can prevent complications from low blood sugar. Monitoring and treatment in the first few days can also prevent complications from high bilirubin levels.
